gist: US death row inmate Christa Pike is unconscious after a failed lethal injection execution.
Lawyers claim prison officials botched the execution by failing to insert IV lines correctly.
Tennessee's governor ordered an independent review and halted all executions for the year.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: US death row inmate Christa Pike is unconscious and on a ventilator following a failed execution attempt. Her lawyers filed an emergency motion to preserve evidence, alleging prison officials botched the lethal injection. They state officials used at least seven needles, bending one, while Pike whimpered and cried. An expert suggested the drug pentobarbital entered tissue under her skin rather than her bloodstream due to ruptured veins or blood clots.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has halted all executions in the state for the year and ordered an independent review. Pike's lawyers had previously warned that her blood-clotting condition and small veins risked causing unnecessary pain.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Authorities have not yet said whether they will attempt to execute Pike again, and her lawyers are seeking to preserve all physical, written, and electronic evidence.

timeline.text: Do humans really have a ‘lizard brain’ lurking beneath our rational minds?

gist: Paul D MacLean proposed the triune brain model in 1959.
The triune model suggests humans have a lizard, mammalian, and rational brain.
Neurobiologists now consider the triune brain model deeply misleading and inaccurate.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: In 1959, Paul D MacLean proposed the triune brain model, suggesting humans possess three layered brains: a primitive lizard brain, a mammalian emotional brain, and a rational neomammalian cortex. This idea became extremely popular.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Neurobiologists now consider the onion-like brain analogy deeply misleading. Evolution does not add neatly divisible mental capacities. Modern anatomical and behavioural evidence shows reptiles possess mammalian features and lower animals solve complex problems.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Despite being discredited by evolutionary and physiological evidence, the triune brain concept endures and is still widely taught in introductory psychology textbooks.

fivew: The triune brain model proposing three layered brains in humans was debunked.

Vintage iPods and modded devices are seeing a resurgence alongside new retro-focused hardware startups.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Portable digital music began in 1998 with early devices like the MPMan F10 and Diamond Rio PMP300. Apple dominated the 2000s with the iPod, capturing over 70 percent of sales. By 2012, smartphones and streaming caused the industry to collapse from $21.6 billion to $613 million.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: A growing anti-streaming sentiment and slowtech trend have sparked renewed interest in offline listening. Vintage iPods fetch high prices on eBay, spawning a modding industry and cheap knockoffs from overseas manufacturers.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: As working used units eventually run out, startups like Sleevenote are attempting fresh concepts. However, a full resurgence on the scale of vinyl remains unlikely due to a lack of collectibility.

fivew: The rise, fall, and resurgence of portable MP3 players.
Consumers are seeking offline listening experiences free from notifications and algorithms.

timeline.text: Money stolen by scammers hijacking UK social media accounts rises 400%

gist: UK losses from hijacked email and social accounts rose over 400% in a year.
Criminals impersonate victims to sell fake gig tickets and solicit emergency money from relatives.
Report Fraud urges people to switch to passkeys to defend against account takeovers.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Report Fraud figures reveal that criminals took £6.3m during 2025-26 by hacking personal email and social accounts, up from £1.2m the previous year. Fraudsters often use stolen profiles to flog bogus tickets to contacts or pose as relatives needing urgent funds.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The true loss is likely far greater because embarrassment and modest sums deter victims from reporting. Breaches quickly spill over, exploiting trust to deceive friends, relatives, and co-workers while locking individuals out of critical services.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Report Fraud is starting a public drive encouraging users to adopt passkeys. These rely on device biometrics rather than passwords, shielding accounts from typical hacking techniques.

timeline.text: Children’s books with Black main characters down 8% in a year, study shows

gist: UK children's books featuring Black main characters fell by nearly eight per cent last year.
Representation of south Asian, Middle Eastern, and disabled characters also declined significantly.
Experts warn that children's books lack incidental representation where identity does not drive plots.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A study by Inclusive Books for Children revealed a decline in diverse main characters in UK books for under-10s in 2025. Books with Black main characters fell by 7.8%, while south Asian representation dropped to 1.4%. Books featuring Middle Eastern and North African characters halved to just three, all of which focused on refugee experiences. Disabled main characters in picture books also fell by 60%.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Experts argue children need stories reflecting their lives to encourage reading. They highlighted a lack of "incidental representation", where diverse characters star in ordinary stories rather than having their identity drive the plot.

Campaigners warn asking past wages maintains historic pay gaps for disadvantaged groups.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Employers are legally permitted to ask job applicants about salary history and salary expectations, though candidates are not required to disclose their pay. Campaigners previously launched #EndSalaryHistory, urging employers to halt the practice. Meanwhile, some interviewees report inflating past pay figures to secure higher wages, despite significant risks.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The Fawcett Society argued that salary history questions perpetuate historical pay inequalities linked to gender, race, and disability. Instead of rewarding skills and experience, employers risk paying candidates based on perceived worth and negotiation abilities.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Advisers suggest applicants state salary expectations, know market rates, and focus on skills, benefits, and their potential contribution.

timeline.text: Holiday cottage company insisted on a death certificate to amend our break

gist: A holiday cottage company demanded a death certificate to amend a booking after a bereavement.
The family faced distressing bureaucratic hurdles and automated emails asking if the deceased enjoyed the stay.
A consumer champion intervened, securing a full refund and a goodwill payment from the company.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A customer died before a family holiday booked with Sykes Holiday Cottages. The company refused to transfer the booking name without formal proof of death, rejecting a marriage certificate, an inquest listing, and a GP letter, while repeatedly emailing the deceased customer.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The company lacked an official bereavement policy and showed a severe lack of empathy during a vulnerable time, imposing onerous requirements for a simple name change.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Following intervention, the company refunded the £2,400 cost plus £150 in goodwill, apologized directly to the family, and stated it is reviewing its processes.

fivew: Sykes Holiday Cottages and a bereaved family.

The company required proof of death to transfer a booking name but mishandled the situation through rigid administrative demands and automated emails.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The separatist Parti Québécois, led by Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, is projected to win a minority government in Quebec's provincial election. This marks the party's first time in power since 2014, following the collapse of the Coalition Avenir Québec.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The victory could test Canadian unity. Plamondon has pledged to hold an independence referendum and challenge the federal government on immigration. He also plans to abolish Quebec's ties to the monarchy, which could trigger legal battles. However, polls suggest only 30% of Quebecers support independence.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: With a minority, Plamondon must seek support from rivals who oppose independence. Outlets differ on the referendum's timing, suggesting either within two years or after US President Donald Trump leaves office.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Two men died after leaving a northern French beach on an overcrowded boat. Rescuers found people bailing water with shoes and dealing with fuel on board. Two women sustained burns from a gasoline and seawater mixture. Meanwhile, protesters gathered in Gosport for a second time, resulting in twelve arrests after violent clashes with police during a rescue operation.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The tragic deaths highlight the ongoing dangers of small boat crossings in the Channel. Additionally, the violent protests in Gosport demonstrate rising unrest and criminal disorder linked to migrant arrivals on the south coast of England.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The public prosecutor's office has launched an investigation to establish how the men died. Authorities have stated they will thoroughly investigate the violent disorder and take strong action against those responsible.

Bulldozers and armoured vehicles are now being deployed as police prepare for an operation.

sections.text: The abduction highlights the severe security risks faced by young people travelling across Nigeria for their national youth service. Kidnappers have demanded a ransom of 50m naira from the families of the victims, placing immense pressure on relatives despite authorities warning that paying ransoms is illegal.

timeline.text: Prisoner took his own life after terror order had 'substantial impact' on mental state, inquest finds

gist: An inquest found terror control measures substantially impacted a prisoner's mental state before death.
Akhtar Uddin died in HMP Wandsworth after being jailed for breaching a TPIM order.
The coroner will issue a report over concerns regarding risks to TPIM subjects.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Akhtar Uddin died in HMP Wandsworth on Christmas Day 2021 whilst serving a sentence for breaching a Terrorism Prevention and Investigation Measure (TPIM). An inquest jury at Inner West London Coroner's Court concluded the restrictive order and fears over its reimposition had a substantial impact on his mental state. They also found the prison service failed to provide the support he needed. Jurors noted it was not possible to determine if he intended his death.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: This was the first inquest to consider the impact of TPIMs. Evidence revealed prison staff had little awareness of the restrictions, leading to unintentionally cruel treatment. The coroner noted the state assessed the risk Uddin posed to others, but not risks to Uddin himself, highlighting a broader lack of support for subjects.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Coroner Bernard Richmond KC stated he will issue a preventing future deaths report to the government because of concerns about risks to others subjected to terrorism control measures.

fivew: An inquest jury concluded that a terrorism control order substantially affected a prisoner's mental state before he took his own life.
He took his own life after facing restrictive measures, fear of their reimposition, and a lack of prison support.

gist: Cooler air, cloud and rain will sweep across the UK from Tuesday.
Temperatures will drop into the mid-teens, ending weeks of unusually warm conditions.
The cooler spell will be short-lived, with temperatures rising again over the weekend.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Cooler air, rain and strong winds are sweeping across the UK from the north-west. Temperatures are falling from the low 20s to the mid-teens, with Wednesday expected to be the first day since 11 June without 20C recorded anywhere in the country.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Although mid-teen temperatures are normal for early October, the contrast with recent unusually warm weather makes the change feel particularly dramatic.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Thursday will start chilly with mist, fog and rural frost before sunshine emerges under temporary high pressure. Atlantic systems will bring further rain and wind on Friday, before temperatures recover towards average at the weekend.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Care proceedings for infants in England have risen by 64% over two decades. Experts warn many babies are taken into care because struggling families lack adequate support.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Most adoptions of infants occur without the written consent of their birth parents. Since early intervention funding has fallen by 44% over a decade, borderline cases are increasingly entering the care system, risking permanent, unnecessary family separations.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: New guidance to reduce short-notice care hearings for newborns will be announced by the end of the year. Additionally, the government is investing £2.4bn to improve early support for families.

timeline.text: ‘Spit on our sacrifice’: Canadian veterans fume after Trump and allies take jibes at military

gist: Canadian veterans and families express anger over recent critical remarks about their military from US figures.
Donald Trump, JD Vance, and other US officials made disparaging comments regarding Canada's defence and contributions.
The remarks have strained diplomatic relations and upset veterans who served alongside US troops.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: US vice-president JD Vance commented that Canada underinvested in its military. Donald Trump's transportation secretary Sean Duffy stated Canada does not have a military, while Pete Hegseth mocked Canadian cadets and a coast guard detachment. Trump previously claimed Canadian and Nato forces in Afghanistan were never needed. Canadian veterans and families condemned these remarks as disrespectful.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The remarks sparked a diplomatic dispute, deeply angering Canadian veterans who fought alongside US troops in Afghanistan and lost comrades. Veterans feel betrayed by the ungrateful attitude after years of close military cooperation.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Some US politicians have attempted to make amends, such as Arizona Democrat senator Rueben Gallego travelling to Ottawa to call the tweets deeply disrespectful. Meanwhile, Canadian veterans are reconsidering their personal ties and future support for the United States.

fivew: Canadian veterans such as Perry Chalmers and Chris Banks, alongside US figures like JD Vance and Donald Trump.
Canadian veterans and families expressed anger after Donald Trump and US allies made disparaging remarks about the Canadian military.
Recently, following comments made by US officials and earlier remarks by Donald Trump.
Veterans feel deeply insulted and betrayed by US criticism after decades of joint military sacrifice and cooperation.

quotes.text: To hear him spit on our sacrifice is insulting, it’s hurtful, and it’s disrespectful to the dead.
What they’re saying is not right.

timeline.text: US households pay 62% more for water than they did a decade ago, study finds

gist: US households pay 62% more for drinking water than a decade ago.
Water prices rose significantly faster than overall inflation, groceries, and incomes.
Corporate-owned water systems charged substantially higher average annual rates than public systems.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A study by Food & Water Watch found that US household drinking water bills increased by 62% over the past decade. The average household using 60,000 gallons paid $531 in 2025. Costs varied greatly by state and ownership, with corporate-owned utilities charging significantly more than publicly owned systems.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Water costs rose faster than inflation, grocery prices, and median household incomes, hitting low-income households the hardest. Experts cited ageing infrastructure, regulatory compliance, and climate change as key cost drivers.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Organizations highlighted the need for infrastructure updates, local affordability programs, and federal support to prevent vulnerable communities from facing severe financial burdens or compromised water safety.

gist: Ofcom is investigating Meta over Instagram's Instants feature under UK safety laws.
The regulator claims Meta failed to conduct proper risk assessments before launching the tool.
Meta insists it conducted a risk analysis and briefed Ofcom before the launch.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Ofcom is investigating Meta for potentially breaching the UK's Online Safety Act. The regulator claims Meta failed to carry out adequate risk assessments regarding illegal content and children's safety before launching Instagram's "Instants" feature in May. Meta states it conducted a risk analysis and briefed Ofcom multiple times before the launch.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Under the Online Safety Act, tech firms must assess risks before launching significant platform changes. Failing to comply can result in formal warnings or fines of up to 10% of global revenue. Meta is already facing other investigations and is legally challenging Ofcom over fees and information demands.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Ofcom's probe will examine if Meta breached its duties. Meta has stated it will co-operate with the investigation.

fivew: The communications regulator Ofcom and tech company Meta.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Russian drone attacks targeting Ukrainian passenger trains have escalated. Passengers describe emergency evacuations, waiting in the dark near explosions, and long delays. sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The attacks disrupt vital transport that has kept Ukraine running since the full-scale invasion, putting passengers and crew members at risk. Russia's defence ministry states it targets infrastructure used for military transport, while the railway operator prioritises passenger safety amid increasingly sophisticated drone technology.

timeline.text: Nobel prize in physics goes to Francis Halzen for south pole work on neutrinos

gist: Belgian physicist Francis Halzen won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics.
He was awarded for his pioneering work on the IceCube Neutrino Observatory.
IceCube detects elusive, high-energy cosmic particles using Antarctic ice.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Belgian physicist Francis Halzen won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded him the prize, worth 12 million Swedish kronor, for his work on the IceCube Neutrino Observatory at the South Pole.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Halzen's work on the observatory, which uses Antarctic ice to detect elusive subatomic particles called neutrinos, has opened up a new kind of astronomy. These high-energy particles act as cosmic messengers, carrying information about violent events in distant galaxies that ordinary telescopes cannot easily see.

gist: A Nigerian military aircraft crashed into a swamp, killing 32 people on board.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A military ATR-42 aircraft crashed into a swamp near a naval base in Ondo State on Monday morning. The plane, carrying 25 passengers and seven crew members, was flying from Benin City to Lagos when it went down. All 32 people on board, mostly military personnel, were killed.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: President Bola Tinubu declared three days of national mourning and ordered flags to fly at half-mast. He described the crash as a painful moment for the nation and its armed forces.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: President Tinubu has ordered a full investigation into the crash. Search and rescue efforts at the site are ongoing.

timeline.text: Kenya confirms its first Ebola death as outbreak spreads

gist: Kenya has confirmed its first ever death from the Ebola virus.
The patient was a Kenyan citizen who had been living in DR Congo.
Health authorities are tracing contacts, including family members and healthcare workers.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Kenya confirmed its first ever Ebola death after a citizen who lived in DR Congo died in Nairobi. The patient travelled from DR Congo via Kampala to Nairobi, where he tested positive for the Bundibugyo species of Ebola and later died.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: This is the first time Ebola has been confirmed in Kenya. The current outbreak in DR Congo, caused by the rare Bundibugyo species, has no approved vaccine or treatment and has killed over 4,000 people this year.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Health authorities are tracing contacts, including 28 identified contacts, 23 passengers, and four crew members from the flight. The patient's burial is planned in line with public health safety protocols.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A 25-year-old UK-Iranian dual national was arrested in Westminster on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts linked to an incident at RAF Fairford and has been released on bail. sections.heading: Why it matters

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The NFL kicked off its London series with a game between the Washington Commanders and Indianapolis Colts. Although one upcoming fixture sold out quickly, thousands of tickets were initially left unsold, prompting the NFL to drop prices and offer discounted or free tickets.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Long-term supporters felt priced out by ticket increases that exceeded inflation and the removal of season-ticket packages. Some fans viewed the changes as a money-grab that alienated loyal attendees in favour of newer consumers.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The NFL continues its international series with upcoming matches in London, featuring teams such as the Philadelphia Eagles and Jacksonville Jaguars.

gist: JJ Gabriel features in Manchester United's official team photo despite efforts to leave.
Europe's top clubs are interested in the teenager as he holds a European Union passport.
His decision to seek a move was triggered by non-inclusion against Sabah FK.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: JJ Gabriel is included in Manchester United's official team photo for the season. The pictures were taken before he informed the club of his intention to leave. His exit decision was triggered by not being included in the squad to face Sabah FK.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Gabriel is a target for several top European clubs, including Real Madrid and Barcelona. Manchester United hold his registration and would consider legal action if illegal inducement emerges.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Gabriel is set to turn 16 and his next involvement in a United game will virtually certainly be as an opposition player.
